Looks like a comprehensive list, thanks for asking!
I'm especially excited to see subsurface scattering and volume rendering in the list.

Only thing I can think of is adding physical camera parameters such as Sensor Size. Being able to set the width & height so it affects the FOV when combined with a Focal Length parameter would make it possible to simulate real world cameras better.
Three.js doesn't really have those parameters exposed, but it does have getter functions for "film height & width" and "focalLength" https://threejs.org/docs/#PerspectiveCamera

> Only thing I can think of is adding physical camera parameters such as Sensor Size ...

Can you explain this a bit more? And maybe give a more specific list of parameters and what's not there? It sounds like "film width", "film height" and "focalLength" are all just different ways to implicitly set the three.js PerspectiveCameras FoV and aspect fields. Is that right? If that's true then the existing fields should "just work" unless I'm misunderstanding something. One thing that could be added is something like a film gate in the render view so if your camera aspect does not match the canvas aspect the view isn't stretched. I've also considered is adding some kind of lens distortion parameter but I don't know how commonly that's used.

For reference you can see some of the existing parameters on the "PhysicalCamera" here for rendering depth of field and bokeh:

https://gkjohnson.github.io/three-gpu-pathtracer/example/bundle/depthOfField.html

The problem with the existing functions is they only **get** the information, but there's no way to **set** "film width", "film height" and "focalLength". Sensor size is sometimes called "film gate" in 3d software, such as Maya, so it sounds we're maybe already talking about the same thing 🙂 A "physical camera" is, in my understanding, just a bit of helper math that makes it easier to use real world values to set the field of view. I think sensor size and focal length could be good additions to your existing physical camera.

Impressive to see the current state of the WebGPUPathTracer, all implemented items, and remaining features listed. 

I'm just commenting to add a reference to a repo, [mbredif/photogrammetric-camera](https://github.com/mbredif/photogrammetric-camera) (and its [itownsResearch fork](https://github.com/itownsResearch/photogrammetric-camera/tree/colmap)) that might be of interest regarding generic threejs cameras by Mathieu Brédif from IGN (french geographic institute), which was also used in a [great thesis](https://theses.hal.science/tel-03697260v1/document) by Evelyn Paiz-Reyes regarding perspective camera models, lens distortion shader-side. 

An often used format to define camera lens intrinsics parameters (focal, distortion etc) is [colmap camera models](https://colmap.github.io/cameras.html), which partly rely on opencv. 
A generic toolbox to convert IO from/to many camera poses extrinsics + intrinsics is available at [naver/kapture](https://github.com/naver/kapture#kapture-tools). In the linked section you also see other camera models formats and specifications.

Came across some videos on material layering that are pretty interesting - could be good to reference how we can introduce custom lobe layering or custom shaders into this project.

Roughness layering for metals: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uz8PIi3ELJg

Layering for surface imperfections: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OW4L0vdo_e4&t=562s

@AntonPalmqvist - do you have any thoughts on what screen effects would be worth supporting? I'm less familiar with what Blender supports but I'm thinking things like bloom, lens flares, and any other types of typical high quality postprocessing effects like this. I know three.js provides a decent quality "Unreal Bloom" but I'm not sure if it's of the quality we'd want for this.

I'm using [react-three-gpu-pathtracer](https://github.com/pmndrs/react-three-gpu-pathtracer) so I have everything from [@react-three/postprocessing](https://react-postprocessing.docs.pmnd.rs/introduction) available to me.

With that said, a more physically accurate bloom and lens flare would be great to have of course, like this one: https://github.com/bean-mhm/realbloom

Here's also a lens flare I recently stumbled upon: https://beatreichenbach.github.io/realflare/

Thanks for asking!

Regarding OIDN on the "Future" list: we shipped an OIDN integration on top of the
WebGL tracer (0.0.24) in a desktop app. OIDN runs natively there, so our code won't
transfer directly, but a few lessons cost us real debugging time and should apply to
any integration.

The biggest one: sanitize NaN/Inf before handing pixels to OIDN, but don't clamp the
range. Path tracing occasionally produces non-finite values and OIDN reacts with
blotches that look like a broken network. Clamping the HDR beauty to [0,1] instead
flattens every highlight. Albedo is the opposite case, it has to be clamped to [0,1].

If the normal AOV comes out of a rasterizer pass it is color-encoded (n * 0.5 + 0.5),
while OIDN wants the raw vector in [-1,1]. We forgot the decode at first and the
denoiser hallucinated edges everywhere.

For large renders we denoise in 2048px tiles with a 96px overlap and only write back
the core of each tile. No visible seams in practice, and memory stays bounded at 4K
and above. And since the input is HDR, we reimplemented OIDN's autoexposure on the
host side (log-average luminance, key 0.18) to feed inputScale. Non-finite pixels
have to count as zero there too, otherwise a single Inf pixel drags the exposure of
the whole frame.

We generate albedo and normals with plain rasterizer passes (material swap, same
camera, tone mapping off) into one shared float target, and keep all readbacks async
so denoising never stalls accumulation. Happy to share more detail when this item
comes up.
